body:
Every humus application is a bedrock.App, and the root package’s humus.App is the lifecycle every humus service runs. It reads its settings, listens for signals, builds its telemetry and the user’s dependencies, runs one or more Services, drains and shuts them down within a grace period, releases what was built, shuts its telemetry down and turns the outcome into an exit status.
A service’s main is func main() { humus.Main(app.Init) }, where app.Init is the end user’s Init. humus.Main builds the humus.App from its defaults and that Init, applies the options it is given, and runs the App on the OS process. Options change the App’s fields, so everything this page says about humus.App is what Main runs. The runtime packages — REST, gRPC, jobs, queues — export Services for Init to return, not Apps, and one whose Services need a drain wraps Main with defaults of its own: see Runtime packages. An App that mixes runtimes, such as a REST API and a gRPC service in one process, needs nothing more.
Telemetry is part of the lifecycle: the App builds it before Init, logs through it, and shuts it down last. See Telemetry below, and the Telemetry page for what a service does with it. Health is a Service like any other: an App’s Init returns the health package’s Service next to its other Services, and Health explains what it does to readiness through the lifecycle.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: the humus App lifecycle and Proposal: humus.Main, with its revision 1 and revision 2. The telemetry integration is in Proposal: OpenTelemetry without globals, Revision 2.
Main humus.Main(init, opts...) runs an App on the OS process and exits the process with the App’s status. It never returns, and only init is required. This main passes the end user’s Init and one option, for its own telemetry:
humus.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) Main builds the App before it runs anything:
It starts from Main’s defaults for Host, Telemetry, ShutdownGracePeriod and Drain. It sets Init to init, so an option sees the end user’s Init and may wrap it, for example to add a Service next to the end user’s. It applies opts in order, so a later option wins over an earlier one. It is then bedrock.Main of that App, the only place a humus program touches the real process. It panics if init or one of opts is nil.
An option is a humus.Option, a func(*humus.App). humus has one for each field Main defaults:
Option Sets humus.WithHost(h) App.Host humus.WithTelemetry(b) App.Telemetry, the App’s telemetry.Builder humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod(d) App.ShutdownGracePeriod, the grace period when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set humus.WithDrain(d) App.Drain, the drain when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set. humus.WithDrain(nil) removes a drain that an earlier option set An option changes exported fields, so an end user or a runtime package can write one of their own as a function literal, and one option may set several fields.
buildTelemetry is the end user’s Builder. It starts from the telemetry package’s defaults, which write log records to standard output, and names the service:
func buildTelemetry(ctx context.Context, p bedrock.Process, dial telemetry.Dialer) (telemetry.SDK, error) { s := telemetry.DefaultSettings() s.ServiceName = "greeter" return telemetry.New(ctx, s, dial, p.Stdout) } A main that wants none of Main’s defaults can still write bedrock.Main(humus.App{…}), and sets every field itself:
bedrock.Main(humus.App{ Host: humus.OSHost(), ShutdownGracePeriod: 30 * time.Second, // when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set Drain: humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second), // when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set Telemetry: buildTelemetry, Init: Init, }) The defaults Field Main’s default Why Host humus.OSHost() Main runs only in main. A test runs its App with humustest.Start, which uses a test Host. Telemetry telemetry.New with telemetry.DefaultSettings(), the Host’s Dial and the Process’s stdout Logs go to stdout as JSON lines, and spans get real IDs without being exported. A service that exports anything passes its own Builder with humus.WithTelemetry. ShutdownGracePeriod 20s It fits inside Kubernetes’ default terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30s, with telemetry’s 5s shutdown after it and a margin for the process to exit. Drain none Only a Service that a load balancer routes to, and that keeps serving until Shutdown, needs a drain, and the package that provides it sets one. The worst case from a signal to the exit is 20s of grace period and 5s of telemetry shutdown, telemetry.Settings.ShutdownTimeout: 25s, inside Kubernetes’ 30s. A drain comes out of the same budget, so a runtime package that sets one shortens its grace period to fit.
The defaults live in Main, not in App. humus.App’s fields keep their meaning: a zero ShutdownGracePeriod fails startup, and a nil Drain doesn’t wait. An operator overrides the grace period and the drain through their variables, whatever Main or an option set, without a rebuild.
Runtime packages A job, a queue consumer and the health Service stop on Serve’s context, so they run on humus.Main’s defaults and need no Main of their own. A runtime package whose Services need a drain, such as an HTTP or gRPC server that keeps serving until Shutdown, wraps Main instead:
It exports its defaults as one humus.Option, so that a test runs with them too. Its Main applies those defaults and then the end user’s options, and calls humus.Main. The end user’s options come last, so they win over the package’s. As a sketch, with the HTTP server foundation’s proposed durations, a 5s drain and a 10s grace period, which fit inside the 25s budget with telemetry’s 5s. That proposal decides the names and the values:
// httpDefaults stands in for a runtime package's defaults, such as // httpserver.Defaults: a 5s drain and a 10s grace period over humus.Main's. func httpDefaults() humus.Option { return func(a *humus.App) { a.Drain = humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second) a.ShutdownGracePeriod = 10 * time.Second } } // httpMain stands in for a runtime package's Main, such as httpserver.Main: // humus.Main with the package's defaults applied before the end user's // options, so that the end user's options win. func httpMain(init func(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error), opts ...humus.Option) { humus.Main(init, append([]humus.Option{httpDefaults()}, opts...)...) } The end user’s main calls the package’s Main, and its test passes the package’s defaults with humustest.WithApp(httpDefaults()), as Testing shows:
httpMain(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) A process picks its Main by what a load balancer routes to. It uses an HTTP or gRPC package’s Main when that server is one a load balancer routes to, as an API next to a job is. A job or a consumer next to a probes or metrics server stays on humus.Main: nothing routes to that server, and a drain would make a finished job wait for the whole delay.
In a mixed process, the package’s budget is everyone’s. A job or a consumer next to a server that is routed to runs on that server’s package’s Main, so its work in flight at a signal gets that package’s drain and grace period: 15s on the HTTP server foundation’s proposed defaults, not humus.Main’s 20s. An end user who needs more passes humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod after the package’s defaults, within the 25s budget. An HTTP and a gRPC server in one process use either package’s Main. Each package’s defaults set both the drain and the grace period, so passing the other package’s defaults as well replaces both: the last one wins.
App An App has five fields:
Field Required Meaning Host yes the network and filesystem the App runs on: humus.OSHost() under Main, and a Host the test controls in a test ShutdownGracePeriod yes, unless HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is set the grace period when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set: 20s under Main. It must be positive, so the zero value fails startup Drain no the drain when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set: a humus.Drain, such as humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second), that runs between shutdown starting and Shutdown being called on the Services, and whose context is done once every Serve has returned. A nil Drain, Main’s default, means no pause Telemetry yes the telemetry.Builder that builds the App’s telemetry: under Main, its default or the end user’s own Builder, and in tests also telemetry.NoopBuilder or the Builder of humustest’s recorder, humustest.Telemetry Init yes builds the App’s dependencies and returns the Services to run ShutdownGracePeriod and Drain are defaults: an operator overrides either through its variable without a rebuild. How long to drain and how long to allow for shutdown depend on what the App runs — a REST or gRPC App needs time for a load balancer to stop sending it connections, and a job does not — so Main has opinions about them, the runtime packages that need other ones set their own, and the App literal has none.
Service A Service is a long-running part of an App: an HTTP server, a gRPC server, a queue consumer or a job. It has two methods, Serve and Shutdown, and the App gives it two shutdown signals, at different times:
Serve’s context is done as soon as the App starts shutting down, before the drain. Shutdown is called after the drain, with the grace period as its context’s deadline. A Service may stop on the first, as a job, a queue consumer or the health Service does: the health Service turns not ready then, so a load balancer stops sending the App new traffic. Or it may keep serving until the second, as an HTTP or gRPC Service does, so that a load balancer still draining connections towards it is answered. This Service keeps serving until Shutdown:
type server struct { out io.Writer ready chan struct{} stopped chan struct{} } func newServer(out io.Writer) *server { return &server{ out: out, ready: make(chan struct{}), stopped: make(chan struct{}), } } func (s *server) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(s.out, "serve: serving") close(s.ready) if err != nil { return err } <-s.stopped return nil } func (s *server) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error { close(s.stopped) _, err := fmt.Fprintln(s.out, "shutdown: stopped serving") return err } Closing ready tells the example that runs it when it is serving. Serve returns nil when Shutdown stopped it or when it finished on its own. Any Service returning from Serve ends the App, so a job is just a Service that returns, and an App is never partly up. Shutdown is called on every Service, including one whose Serve has already returned, so it must be safe to call then. If its context is done before the Service has stopped, Shutdown stops it at once and returns an error that wraps the context’s error.
The drain The drain is the pause between shutdown starting and Shutdown being called on the Services, so that load balancers stop sending the App new work before its servers stop. It is a function, humus.Drain, so that what it waits for is the end user’s choice, and so that it can stop waiting once nothing is left to drain: a func(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) error. App.Drain holds it. Main sets none, and a nil Drain means no pause.
It ends once every Serve has returned. Run calls the Drain after Serve’s context is done, when it hasn’t yet received every Serve’s result, with the Setup that Init was given. The Drain’s context is done once every Service’s Serve has returned, because nothing is left to drain. A Service that stops on Serve’s context returns at once or once its work in flight is done, and a Service that keeps serving until Shutdown doesn’t return until after the drain. So, for an App with a Drain set:
The App’s Services The drain lasts a job, finished on its own nothing: Run doesn’t call the Drain a job, finished on its own, next to the health Service nothing: Run calls the Drain, and its context is done at once a job, interrupted by a signal until the run returns, at most the Drain’s delay a queue consumer until its records in flight are done, at most the Drain’s delay an HTTP or gRPC server, with or without the health Service the Drain’s whole delay a job and an HTTP server the Drain’s whole delay, unless both return first On humus.Main’s defaults there is no Drain, so none of these drain. An Init that returns no Services ends the App without a drain too, because there is nothing to drain.
humus.DrainDelay(d) is the usual kind of drain. It waits d, or until its context is done, and returns nil either way. A runtime package that needs a drain sets one in its defaults, and an end user passes one with humus.WithDrain(humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second)). It doesn’t look at the shutdown’s cause: after a Service returned on its own, it still gives load balancers its delay to notice that the pod is no longer ready. It panics if d is negative.
A Drain returns nil when its context is done. A done context is how a Drain learns that nothing is left to drain, which is a normal end, not a failure: a Drain that returns ctx.Err() then fails the App, with drain: context canceled in the cause. Run may call a Drain whose context is done at once, as for a finished job next to the health Service, so a Drain checks its context before it acts. A Drain returns when it is done or when its context is done, whichever comes first.
The Drain is not bounded by the grace period. Run waits for it to return, and the grace period starts after it. A Drain that ignores its context holds the App up until a second signal, or Kubernetes’ SIGKILL, ends the process. Its context keeps the values of Run’s context but is not cancelled with it. An error it returns is logged at ERROR, joined into the App’s cause as drain: and the error, and exits 1, and Shutdown is still called on every Service.
A Drain of the end user’s own checks ShutdownCause before it waits on a load balancer. humus.ShutdownCause(ctx) says why the shutdown started: after a signal, it is the signal’s cause, and Kubernetes is terminating the pod and removing it from load balancers. When a Service returned on its own first, such as a job next to an API, it wraps humus.ErrServiceReturned, and nothing outside is draining the App. A Drain that waited for deregistration then would wait for something nothing triggers. This Drain polls a load balancer through s.Host.Dial, so that it runs on a test Host too, and only after a signal:
func deregisteringDrain(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) error { if errors.Is(humus.ShutdownCause(ctx), humus.ErrServiceReturned) { return nil // no signal came, so nothing is deregistering the pod } return waitUntilDeregistered(ctx, s.Host.Dial) } waitUntilDeregistered returns nil when ctx is done. The end user passes the Drain with humus.WithDrain:
humus.Main(Init, humus.WithDrain(deregisteringDrain)) The Drain gets the Setup, not what Init built, because it is chosen in main, before Init runs. Work at shutdown that needs Init’s dependencies, such as deregistering from service discovery, belongs in a Service that stops on Serve’s context: it sees shutdown start at the same moment, and the Drain then waits for whatever has to follow it.
HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY replaces any Drain. When it is set, Run uses humus.DrainDelay of its value in place of App.Drain, whatever that is, and adds a drain to an App that has none. An operator can always replace a Drain that misbehaves, from the same manifest that sets terminationGracePeriodSeconds. See Settings.
Host A Host is what humus hands an App beyond its process: Listen, Dial and a filesystem, FS. Every field is required. Under humus.Main an App runs on humus.OSHost(), which is net.Listen, a net.Dialer’s DialContext, and an FS that calls package os directly. In a test it runs on a Host whose listeners, dialler and filesystem the test controls, so that a whole App runs without touching the real host.
Host is meant for user code as well as for humus. Hand Host.Dial to a client that takes a dial function, such as pgx’s DialFunc, and open files through Host.FS rather than through package os.
Why FS hands out *os.File FS names files by OS path and opens them as *os.File, rather than through an in-memory filesystem:
Libraries that need a real file or a path keep working in a test: SQLite drivers, archive libraries, programs started with os/exec. There is no fake filesystem to build and keep in line with the real one. It is a one-way decision. An *os.File is always an OS handle, so moving to an in-memory filesystem later would change every signature. OSHost’s FS is not os.OpenRoot("/"), because an os.Root refuses to follow absolute symbolic links even when it is rooted at /, and paths on a real host routinely pass through them.
What it costs a test: the rule is that it opens no file outside its own temporary directory; it cannot make a write fail with a full disk, so code that needs that test puts an io.Writer seam in its own code; and file modification times are real under synctest, so code that compares ModTime() with time.Now() needs Chtimes in its tests.
Setup and OnStop Init is given a *humus.Setup holding the bedrock.Process the App is run with, the App’s Host and its telemetry, Setup.Telemetry. Init reads its configuration from Setup.Process, builds its dependencies on Setup.Host, takes their tracers, meters and loggers from Setup.Telemetry, and returns the Services to run. Its context is done when the App receives an interrupt or SIGTERM, so a slow Init, such as one retrying a database connection, is cancelled by a signal.
Setup.OnStop registers a function that releases something Init built. The functions work like t.Cleanup: they run in reverse order of registration once every Service has stopped, and they run when Init fails partway through too. So register each release as soon as the thing it releases is built:
func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { out := s.Process.Stdout s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(out, "on stop: close the cache") return err }) s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(out, "on stop: close the queue") return err }) if _, err := config.Env(s.Process.Environment, "DATABASE_URL").Read(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78: init: config DATABASE_URL: not found } return []humus.Service{newServer(out)}, nil } Run without DATABASE_URL, this App closes the queue and then the cache, logs init: config DATABASE_URL: not found at ERROR through its telemetry, and exits 78.
The OnStop functions share the grace period with the Services’ Shutdown: the context each is given is done when the grace period runs out.
What Run does, in order Reads the lifecycle’s settings from the process’s environment, defaulting each to its App field: under Main, that is Main’s default, or what an option set. A malformed one, or a bad default, exits 78 before the App listens for signals, and Init is never called. Listens for an interrupt and SIGTERM through the process’s NotifyContext, before the telemetry and Init, so a signal during a slow Builder or a slow Init cancels it. Builds the telemetry by calling App.Telemetry. If it fails, Init is never called, and the App exits 78 when a *config.Error is in the error chain, or 1 otherwise. Sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler, which writes each export error to standard error. Calls Init. If it fails, runs the OnStop functions registered so far, within the grace period, and exits 78 when a *config.Error is in Init’s error chain, or 1 otherwise. Calls Serve on every Service concurrently, and logs serving. Waits for a signal, or for the first Service to return. Stops listening for signals, so that a second interrupt or SIGTERM takes its default action and ends the process at once, cancels the context passed to Serve, and logs shutting down. When it hasn’t yet received every Serve’s result, calls the drain, with the Setup that Init was given: humus.DrainDelay of HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY when that is set, and App.Drain otherwise. Its context keeps the values of Run’s context but is not cancelled with it, is done once every Serve has returned, and gives humus.ShutdownCause why the shutdown started. Run collects the Serve results that arrive in the meantime and waits for the drain to return. A drain error is logged at ERROR and joined into the cause as drain: and the error. Calls Shutdown on every Service concurrently, waits for every Serve to return, and then runs the OnStop functions in reverse order of registration. All of this happens within one grace period, HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, which starts after the drain. Then it logs stopped. Shuts the telemetry down. Returns the exit status. An Init that returns no Services, and a Service that returns on its own when it is the only one, end the App without calling the drain, as there is nothing to drain. A cancelled root context still gets a graceful shutdown: the grace period keeps the context’s values but not its cancellation. Every failure is the cause of the exit status. Once the telemetry is built, each failure is logged through it, one record per error; before that, it is written to standard error, one line per error. The lifecycle never recovers a panic.
Telemetry App.Telemetry is the App’s telemetry.Builder, and it is required. Main’s default calls telemetry.New with telemetry.DefaultSettings(), so log records go to standard output as JSON lines and nothing is exported. A service that exports anything passes its own Builder with humus.WithTelemetry, such as buildTelemetry above, which sources telemetry.Settings however it likes and calls telemetry.New. A test run with humustest.Start keeps Main’s default unless it passes telemetry.NoopBuilder, or the Builder of humustest’s recorder, humustest.Telemetry, when the test asserts on what the App emits. Telemetry explains how to write the Builder, what the defaults are, the console log format, and how logs get their trace context.
Telemetry is built after NotifyContext and before Init. Run calls App.Telemetry with the context that a signal cancels, the Process, and the Host’s Dial, so the OTLP exporters reach the collector through the Host. A Builder that runs a resource detector can be slow, because a cloud detector calls its metadata server, so a signal cancels it as it cancels a slow Init. A failure exits 78 when a *config.Error is in its chain, such as a malformed variable the Builder read, and 1 otherwise. A Builder that returns an SDK with a nil field fails too, and exits 1. In every case Init is never called. Init gets the SDK in Setup.Telemetry, and hands it on to its Services.
Failures are logged through telemetry. The lifecycle logs with the OpenTelemetry Logs API, through Setup.Telemetry.LoggerProvider.Logger("github.com/z5labs/humus"): its own records, serving, shutting down and stopped, at INFO, and every failure after the telemetry is built at ERROR, one record per error, so an operator sees them in the same log stream as everything else. humus has no logging bridge of its own. Standard error still gets what telemetry cannot report itself:
a failure to build telemetry, and a malformed lifecycle setting, which come before there is any telemetry; export errors, each on one line starting with telemetry: . Run sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler to write them there, because a failing exporter cannot report its own failure; a failure to shut telemetry down. Telemetry shuts down last: after the OnStop functions, or after a failed Init and its OnStop functions. So the spans and logs that record a slow or failed shutdown are still exported. Its context keeps the root context’s values but not its cancellation, and it is separate from the grace period: telemetry.New bounds it with Settings.ShutdownTimeout. A failure to shut telemetry down is joined into the cause of the exit status, and it turns an exit 0 into 1.
Settings Variable Default Meaning HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD App.ShutdownGracePeriod: Main’s 20s, unless an option sets another bounds the whole shutdown: every Service’s Shutdown and every OnStop function share it. A time.ParseDuration string, such as 30s, that must be positive. HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY App.Drain: none under Main, unless an option sets one the drain, in place of App.Drain, whatever that is, including none: humus.DrainDelay of a time.ParseDuration string, such as 5s, that must not be negative; 0s means no pause. These are the only variables the lifecycle reads, and the root package is the one place humus reads them. Each value is checked after its default, so a bad default fails the same way as a bad variable: an App whose ShutdownGracePeriod is zero, run without HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, exits 78 with config HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD: must be positive. When both values are bad, both are reported, one line each.
Exit codes Code When Cause 0 a signal stopped the App and it shut down in time the signal 0 a Service returned nil on its own, and the App shut down in time none 1 (humus.ExitFailure) the telemetry could not be built, or its SDK has a nil field the error 1 (humus.ExitFailure) Init, a Service, a Service’s Shutdown, an OnStop function or the telemetry’s shutdown failed every error, joined 1 (humus.ExitFailure) the shutdown ran past the grace period a *humus.GracePeriodError 2 never set by humus: Go’s exit status for an unrecovered panic 78 (humus.ExitConfig) a setting is missing or malformed, including a config value read by the telemetry Builder or by Init a *config.Error in the chain 78 is EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h. It tells an operator “fix the configuration” apart from “the service failed”. Everything else that fails exits 1, and a test tells those failures apart by their cause: errors.AsType[*config.Error] for a config error, and errors.AsType[*humus.GracePeriodError] for a shutdown that ran out of time. A flag usage error is an Init failure and exits 1.
Testing a whole App An App runs whole inside a test. humustest.Start runs the App that Main would run for an Init, with Main’s defaults, on a test Host in place of humus.OSHost() and on a fake process from bedrocktest, whose arguments and environment the test sets, whose output the test reads, and to which the test sends fake signals. Options given with humustest.WithApp change the App as they would in main. testing/synctest runs it in fake time, so a five-second drain passes at once and is measured exactly. The lifecycle’s own tests run it with fake Services:
type fakeService struct { serve func(ctx context.Context) error shutdown func(ctx context.Context) error mu sync.Mutex shutdownCalls int } func (s *fakeService) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { if s.serve == nil { <-ctx.Done() return nil } return s.serve(ctx) } func (s *fakeService) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error { s.mu.Lock() s.shutdownCalls++ s.mu.Unlock() if s.shutdown == nil { return nil } return s.shutdown(ctx) } This test runs an App with an HTTP-like Service and a consumer through a whole lifecycle, from SIGTERM to the OnStop functions, with a 5s drain:
func TestStart_a_whole_App(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { // api keeps serving until Shutdown, as an HTTP server does. stopped := make(chan struct{}) var shutdownAt time.Time api := &fakeService{ serve: func(context.Context) error { <-stopped return nil }, shutdown: func(context.Context) error { shutdownAt = time.Now() close(stopped) return nil }, } // consumer stops as soon as Serve's context is done, as a queue // consumer does. var consumerStoppedAt time.Time consumer := &fakeService{serve: func(ctx context.Context) error { <-ctx.Done() consumerStoppedAt = time.Now() return nil }} var poolClosedAt time.Time init := func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { poolClosedAt = time.Now() return nil }) return []humus.Service{api, consumer}, nil } p, status := humustest.Start(t, init, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithDrain(humus.DrainDelay(5*time.Second))), ) <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) synctest.Wait() // every Serve has started sigterm := time.Now() p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status if st.Code() != 0 { t.Errorf("code = %d, want 0: %v", st.Code(), st.Cause()) } if !errors.Is(st.Cause(), context.Canceled) { t.Errorf("cause = %v, want the signal", st.Cause()) } if got := consumerStoppedAt.Sub(sigterm); got != 0 { t.Errorf("consumer stopped %s after SIGTERM, want at once", got) } if got := shutdownAt.Sub(sigterm); got != 5*time.Second { t.Errorf("Shutdown called %s after SIGTERM, want after the 5s drain", got) } if api.calls() != 1 || consumer.calls() != 1 { t.Errorf("Shutdown called %d and %d times, want once each", api.calls(), consumer.calls()) } if poolClosedAt.IsZero() || poolClosedAt.Before(shutdownAt) { t.Errorf("OnStop ran at %v, want it after Shutdown at %v", poolClosedAt, shutdownAt) } if got := p.Stderr(); got != "" { t.Errorf("stderr = %q, want nothing", got) } }) } synctest reports a deadlock when a goroutine the App started outlives the test body, which makes it a leak detector for Services. For an HTTP Service the cost is that handlers must honour r.Context(), because a handler that ignores it after the server force-closes the connection outlives the test.
Testing a humus App covers humustest.Start in full, and runs Apps that serve real HTTP, on a humustest Host whose network and filesystem the test controls.
Ambient leaks Some dependencies read the real process behind an App’s back, so they reach around the bedrock.Process and the Host an App is given, and a test can neither control nor see what they read. Avoid them, or configure them explicitly from Setup:
pgx reads the real process. pgx.ParseConfig and pgxpool.ParseConfig take every setting the connection string leaves out from PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD and the other PG* variables of the real environment, and default the user to the OS user. They read the password file that PGPASSFILE names, or ~/.pgpass, from the real disk and use it when the connection string sets no password, and they pick up client certificates from ~/.postgresql. The config they return dials the real network: set cfg.ConnConfig.DialFunc = s.Host.Dial before opening the pool. Its LookupFunc still resolves host names with the real resolver. flag.CommandLine and flag.ExitOnError read os.Args and exit the process. Parse p.Args[1:] with a flag.FlagSet of your own, using flag.ContinueOnError. An exec.Cmd with a nil Env inherits the real environment. Build its Env from the keys you know, reading each through p.Environment. http.ProxyFromEnvironment, the Proxy of http.DefaultTransport, reads the proxy variables of the real environment, and http.DefaultClient dials the real network rather than through Host.Dial. slog.Default writes to the real standard error unless it is replaced, and replacing it is process-wide state. OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler, which Run sets. In a process with several Apps, the last App to start gets every App’s export errors, so a test that asserts on export errors does not run in parallel. OpenTelemetry’s internal logger, which writes its own errors to the real standard error. OTEL_GO_X_*, OpenTelemetry’s experimental features, which the SDK reads from the real environment. Any resource detector the end user opts into in Settings.ResourceOptions, which reads the real host, such as /etc, /proc and cgroups, or dials a metadata server rather than through Host.Dial. flag, exec.Cmd, http.ProxyFromEnvironment and slog.Default are on bedrock’s own list. A dependency found reading the real process belongs on this list.

A service reports its health as monitors it combines into two probes, liveness and readiness, and an App’s readiness is owned by a health Service it returns from Init like any other Service. All of it is in the health package, which depends on nothing but the standard library.
The design behind this page is in Proposal: health monitors and probes, Revision 2.
Monitors A Monitor is anything that can report whether it is healthy right now: a database ping, a flag the service sets once it has started, a check of a queue’s depth. It has one method, Healthy(ctx context.Context) (bool, error), which returns false, or an error, when the monitor is not healthy. Two monitors come with the package:
Binary is a monitor the service marks healthy or unhealthy itself, with MarkHealthy and MarkUnhealthy. Its zero value is unhealthy, and it is safe for concurrent use. MonitorFunc turns any func(context.Context) (bool, error) into a monitor. Its Healthy calls the function with the context it is given. A monitor honours the ctx it is given. Whatever checks a monitor, such as an orchestrator’s probe with a timeout, bounds the check with that context, so a monitor that dials or queries something passes ctx on rather than using a context of its own. A database ping that ignores it can hang a probe past its deadline.
Combining monitors Monitors combine, and the combinations are monitors themselves, so they nest:
And is healthy when every one of its monitors is. It checks them in order and stops at the first failure, the first monitor that is unhealthy or returns an error, and returns that monitor’s result without checking the rest. And with no monitors is healthy. Or is healthy when any one of its monitors is. It stops at the first that is healthy; otherwise it is unhealthy and joins the errors every monitor returned, with errors.Join. Or with no monitors is unhealthy. Both pass the context they are given to every monitor they check, nested ones included, so a caller’s deadline reaches each check.
Liveness and readiness An orchestrator such as Kubernetes asks a service two questions, and Probes holds a monitor for each:
Probe Question When it fails, Kubernetes Liveness is the process still working? restarts the container Readiness can the process serve traffic right now? stops sending it traffic until the probe passes again, without restarting it So a liveness probe should fail only when a restart would fix the process, a deadlock for example. Liveness checks no dependencies by default, which is And with no monitors: restarting a pod doesn’t fix a database that is down, and a liveness probe that checks one restarts every pod of the service while the database is down. Dependency checks go in readiness, which takes the pod out of the load balancer until the database is back.
Here readiness checks that the service has started and that its database answers ping, and liveness checks nothing:
var started health.Binary probes := health.Probes{ Liveness: health.And(), Readiness: health.And(&started, health.MonitorFunc(func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) { return ping(ctx) == nil, nil })), } The health Service A health.Service is a Service that owns an App’s readiness. The end user’s Init builds one with NewService, adds monitors to its probes with Liveness and Readiness, and returns it next to the App’s other Services:
Init: func(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { hs := health.NewService( health.Liveness(&working), health.Readiness(health.MonitorFunc(func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) { return ping(ctx) == nil, nil })), ) probes <- hs.Probes() // where an HTTP or gRPC Service would expose them return []humus.Service{hs}, nil }, Service.Probes returns its probes. Readiness is And of the Service’s own state and the monitors Readiness added, in the order they were added, so no monitor is checked while the Service itself is not ready. Liveness is And of the monitors Liveness added, and is healthy when there are none. The probes report the Service’s state when they are checked, so Probes may be called before the App runs. Liveness and Readiness panic on a nil monitor.
Readiness through the lifecycle The Service’s own readiness follows the lifecycle:
Not ready until it is serving. It is not ready from NewService until the App calls its Serve. Ready while it serves, as long as its readiness monitors are healthy. Not ready from the moment shutdown starts, through the drain. The App cancels Serve’s context as soon as it starts shutting down, before the drain, and the Service turns not ready then, for good. A load balancer checking readiness stops sending the App new traffic while the App’s HTTP and gRPC Services, which keep serving until Shutdown, answer what is still draining towards them. So the health Service is one of the Services that stop on the first shutdown signal: its Serve returns as soon as its context is done. A Service is served once; a Serve called after Shutdown, or after an earlier Serve, returns at once and leaves it not ready.
A health Service built but not returned from Init never turns ready. humus.App runs only the Services Init returns, so a Service it is never handed is never served, and its readiness probe fails for as long as the process lives. If an App’s readiness never passes, check that its health Service is in the slice Init returns.
Jobs A job needs no health Service. humus.App runs only the Services Init returns, and nothing in the lifecycle asks for readiness, so a job’s Init returns the job and nothing else. A job runs to completion rather than serving traffic, so there is nothing for a load balancer to route to it.
Exposing the probes The health Service serves no protocol: nothing in the health package opens a port or answers an orchestrator’s probes. Its Probes are monitors, and whatever exposes them calls Healthy on them. Serving them over HTTP and gRPC is planned in wave 4 of the charter, and isn’t available yet.
Testing A health Service is tested in a whole App, with bedrocktest’s fake process and a humustest Host, under testing/synctest, so the drain passes in fake time and readiness can be checked while it runs. This is health’s own test that the Service is not ready during the drain:
func TestServiceIsNotReadyDuringTheDrainDelay(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { hs := health.NewService() readiness := hs.Probes().Readiness api := newServer() // keeps serving, so the drain lasts its whole delay app := humus.App{ Host: humustest.NewHost(t).Host(), Telemetry: telemetry.NoopBuilder, ShutdownGracePeriod: 10 * time.Second, Drain: humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second), Init: func(context.Context, *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { return []humus.Service{api, hs}, nil }, } p := bedrocktest.NewProcess(t) status := make(chan bedrock.ExitStatus, 1) go func() { status <- app.Run(t.Context(), p.Process()) }() <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) synctest.Wait() // Serve has started ready, err := readiness.Healthy(t.Context()) require.NoError(t, err) require.True(t, ready) sigterm := time.Now() p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) synctest.Wait() // shutdown has started; the drain is running ready, err = readiness.Healthy(t.Context()) require.NoError(t, err) require.False(t, ready) require.Zero(t, (<-status).Code()) require.Equal(t, 5*time.Second, time.Since(sigterm)) }) } <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) waits until the App listens for signals, and synctest.Wait until every goroutine in the test, Serve included, is blocked, so the first check sees the Service serving. After the SIGTERM, synctest.Wait returns while the App waits out its five-second drain, and readiness is already false. The drain ends once every Serve has returned, and the health Service’s Serve returns as soon as shutdown starts, so the test runs it next to api, a Service that keeps serving until Shutdown as an HTTP or gRPC Service does: that is what keeps the drain running for its whole five seconds. A test of an App’s own readiness monitors works the same way: take the probes from the Service, run the App, and check them at each point of the lifecycle.

A job is a process that does one piece of work and exits. The job package turns that work, the run, into a humus.Service that runs it once, stops it on either shutdown signal and records one span around it. The job runs on humus.Main’s defaults, and the run’s error is the exit status, so Kubernetes retries a job that failed or was interrupted and completes one that finished.
The package is job.NewService and nothing else: no App, no Main, no Settings. The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: jobs and its revision.
The run A job’s work is its run: a plain func(ctx context.Context) error. A type with a Run method passes its method value, e.Run, so the package has no interface to implement and no adapter to wrap it in. This run exports to a bucket, and returns early with its context’s error when the context is done:
// exporter is the end user's job. Its Run method is the run. type exporter struct { bucket string out io.Writer } // Run does the job's work once, and returns early with ctx's error when ctx // is done, so that an interrupted run exits 1. func (e *exporter) Run(ctx context.Context) error { if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil { return err } _, err := fmt.Fprintln(e.out, "exported to", e.bucket) return err } The end user’s Init builds the run’s dependencies, releases them with s.OnStop, and returns job.NewService(s, run) to humus.Main. Here the dependency is a buffered writer, flushed once the job has stopped:
// Init is the end user's Init: it builds the run's dependencies, releases // them with s.OnStop, and returns the job's Service. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { bucket, err := config.Env(s.Process.Environment, "EXPORT_BUCKET").Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78 } out := bufio.NewWriter(s.Process.Stdout) s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { return out.Flush() }) e := &exporter{bucket: bucket, out: out} return []humus.Service{job.NewService(s, e.Run)}, nil } The job’s main is one call to humus.Main, here with a telemetry Builder that names the service:
humus.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) The Service’s Serve calls the run once, on Serve’s own goroutine, and returns when the run does. A Service returning on its own ends the App, so the job finishing ends the process. A Serve called a second time, or after Shutdown, returns nil without running the job again.
The defaults A job runs on humus.Main’s defaults, which are a job’s, so job has no Main and no defaults of its own:
A grace period of 20s. It fits inside Kubernetes’ default terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30s, with room for the telemetry’s 5s shutdown after it. No drain. Nothing routes traffic to a job, so there is nothing to wait for: after a signal, Shutdown is called on the job straight away. An operator changes the grace period with HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, such as HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD=45s, without a rebuild, and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY adds a drain, as for any App. A main that wants a different default in code passes humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod to humus.Main; the variable still wins over it. The lifecycle’s settings describes both variables.
Exit statuses job adds no exit codes. The lifecycle’s apply, and the run decides which:
The run Exit Cause returns nil 0 none returns an error 1 serve: and the run’s error is interrupted by a signal, and returns ctx’s error 1 serve: context canceled, or the signal when the run returns context.Cause(ctx) is interrupted by a signal, but returns nil 0 the signal ignores its context past the grace period 1 a *humus.GracePeriodError panics 2 none: Go’s runtime prints the panic and exits Init fails reading a setting 78 the *config.Error A run that a signal interrupts exits 1 unless it returns nil. So Kubernetes counts the pod as failed and retries the unfinished work, rather than completing the Job. A run that stops early because its context is done returns ctx.Err(), as almost all Go code already does, and as Run above does: the cause is then serve: context canceled. A run that wants the signal in its cause returns context.Cause(ctx) instead, and the cause is then, for example, serve: terminated signal received.
The fourth row is the run’s own decision. A run that returns nil after a signal has either finished its work or chosen to treat stopping early as done, and the Job completes.
Kubernetes A Kubernetes Job reads the exit code of its pod’s container, and the exit statuses above are chosen for what it does with each.
backoffLimit and restartPolicy Exit 0 completes the Job. The container terminated successfully, so the pod is Succeeded and counts towards the Job’s completions, one by default.
Every other code is a failure, 1, 2 and 78 alike. The Job retries it until it has failed backoffLimit times, 6 by default, with an exponential back-off between attempts, and then marks the Job failed. How it retries depends on the pod template’s restartPolicy, which must be OnFailure or Never for a Job:
OnFailure: the kubelet restarts the container in the same pod, so the job’s next attempt reuses the pod and its volumes. Never: the pod stays Failed, and the Job starts a new pod for the next attempt. A pod failure policy, below, needs Never. So with the defaults alone, a job whose configuration is wrong is retried six times, and a job that an eviction interrupted counts that interruption against the same limit as a real failure.
A pod failure policy A podFailurePolicy tells those cases apart. This one fails the Job at once on exit 78, since a retry reads the same bad setting, and ignores disruptions, the evictions, preemptions and deletions that Kubernetes marks with the DisruptionTarget pod condition. An ignored failure is retried with a new pod and is not counted against backoffLimit:
apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job metadata: name: exporter spec: backoffLimit: 6 podFailurePolicy: rules: - action: FailJob onExitCodes: containerName: exporter operator: In values: [78] - action: Ignore onPodConditions: - type: DisruptionTarget template: spec: restartPolicy: Never terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 containers: - name: exporter image: registry.example.com/exporter:1.0.0 env: - name: EXPORT_BUCKET value: nightly The rules are checked in order, and the first that matches applies. A pod whose run an eviction interrupted exits 1, which the first rule does not match, and has the DisruptionTarget condition, which the second does. Any other failure, such as a run that returned an error or panicked, matches neither and counts against backoffLimit as before. That is why humus has no exit code of its own for an interruption: the condition already tells an interruption apart from a failure.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds When Kubernetes stops a pod, it sends the container SIGTERM, and then SIGKILL once terminationGracePeriodSeconds have passed, 30 by default. A job has to be gone by then. On humus.Main’s defaults, the worst case from SIGTERM to the exit is the 20s grace period and the telemetry’s shutdown, telemetry.Settings.ShutdownTimeout, 5s: 25s, inside Kubernetes’ 30s.
A job that raises HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD raises terminationGracePeriodSeconds with it, to at least the grace period plus the telemetry’s shutdown plus a margin for the process to exit. Otherwise SIGKILL ends the job first: its container exits 137, the process is killed before it runs its OnStop functions, and the telemetry it had not yet exported is lost.
The two signals The App gives a Service two signals to stop on, and the run stops on either:
Serve’s context. The run’s context is made from Serve’s, which is done as soon as the App starts shutting down. So a signal cancels the run at once, and the run has the grace period to stop. Shutdown. Shutdown cancels the run’s context too, and waits for Serve to return. In an App, Serve’s context is always done first, so this matters only when a caller calls Shutdown first, as humustest.TestService does. Serve then returns nil for a run that returns a cancellation, because the Service contract says a Service that Shutdown stopped returns nil. Which signal came first decides what Serve returns. After a signal, it returns the run’s error, unchanged, and the App exits 1. After a bare Shutdown, it returns nil when the run’s error is a cancellation, and the run’s error otherwise.
Telemetry The job span Each run has one span, named job, of kind internal, from the TracerProvider of the Setup’s telemetry. When the run returns an error, the span’s status is Error with the error’s text, including when Serve reports a run that Shutdown stopped as nil: the span records what the run returned.
The run’s context carries the span. So every span the run starts from that context is its child, and every record it logs with that context carries its trace ID. This Init takes a tracer and a logger from s.Telemetry, and its run uses both with the run’s context:
tracer := s.Telemetry.TracerProvider.Tracer("exporter") logger := otelslog.NewLogger("exporter", otelslog.WithLoggerProvider(s.Telemetry.LoggerProvider)) return []humus.Service{job.NewService(s, func(ctx context.Context) error { _, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "export") defer span.End() logger.InfoContext(ctx, "exported") return nil })}, nil The export span is a child of job, and the exported record carries the job span’s trace ID. With telemetry.DefaultSettings() traces are not exported, but spans still get real IDs, so one job’s console logs share a trace ID without a collector. job writes no log records and records no metrics of its own: the lifecycle already logs serving, shutting down, stopped and a failed Serve, and the orchestrator sees every run, including the ones that never started.
Joining the trace that started the job A job is often started by a process that is itself traced, such as a workflow engine or a CI step. OpenTelemetry’s environment-variable carriers have that process pass its trace context to the job in environment variables, and the run’s span joins it.
Serve extracts a trace context from the Process’s environment with the Builder’s propagator, s.Telemetry.Propagator, and the run’s span is that context’s child, still of kind internal. Each of the propagator’s keys is read under the name the specification gives it: ASCII letters uppercased, and every character but an ASCII letter, digit or _ replaced with _. So:
With telemetry.New’s propagator, W3C trace context and baggage, the variables are TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE. With a propagator of another kind, from a Builder of your own, such as B3, they are that propagator’s keys, read the same way: x-b3-traceid as X_B3_TRACEID. humus defines none of these names: the propagator’s keys and the specification do. The extracted context is the parent of the run’s span and of nothing else, so the spans Init starts stay in traces of their own. Its baggage is on the run’s context, and the run reads it with baggage.FromContext(ctx):
schedule = baggage.FromContext(ctx).Member("schedule").Value() A new trace when none is set When none of the variables is set, or the trace context in them is malformed, the run’s span is the root of a new trace, with no error and nothing logged, as for an HTTP request with a bad traceparent header.
Kubernetes sets none of these variables. A Job or a CronJob’s run starts a new trace on every run, unless the pod spec sets TRACEPARENT itself or whatever creates the Job passes its own.
More than the job A process that runs a job next to other Services, such as the health Service or a metrics server, returns them all from the end user’s Init, with the job’s among them:
run := func(context.Context) error { return nil } return []humus.Service{ health.NewService(), job.NewService(s, run), }, nil Any Service returning ends the App, so the job finishing ends the process, and the other Services with it.
Which Main the process uses depends on what a load balancer routes to, as the lifecycle’s runtime packages explains for mixed processes:
Next to a probes or metrics server, a job stays on humus.Main. Nothing routes to that server, and a drain would make a finished job wait for the whole delay. Next to a server a load balancer routes to, such as an API, the process uses that server’s package’s Main. After a signal, the run then gets that package’s drain and grace period rather than humus.Main’s. What job leaves to you Retries inside a run. Kubernetes retries a failed pod under backoffLimit. A run that wants to retry one step in the process, such as a call to a flaky API, uses whatever it likes inside the run, such as bedrock’s retry module. job doesn’t wrap it, so the retries stay visible in your code. Idempotency across Kubernetes’ retries. An interrupted or failed run is run again from the start, in a new process, so a run that half finished must be safe to run again: write with upserts, skip what is already done, or record progress somewhere the next attempt reads it. Panics. job recovers no panic. A run that panics crashes the process with Go’s exit status 2 and the stack trace on stderr, which Kubernetes counts as a failure and retries under backoffLimit. A run that wants a panic reported differently recovers it itself. Testing A job is tested whole, with humustest.Start, inside testing/synctest, as Testing a humus App describes for any App. The tests below use a helper, runs, which returns an Init whose only Service is a job that runs the given run:
// runs returns an Init whose only Service is a job that runs run. func runs(run func(context.Context) error) func(context.Context, *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { return func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { return []humus.Service{job.NewService(s, run)}, nil } } A whole job, and SIGTERM humustest.Start returns the test’s process, and p.Signal sends it a signal, as Kubernetes sends SIGTERM. synctest.Wait lets the run block on its context first, and fake time means the grace period costs the test nothing:
func TestService_SIGTERM_interrupts_the_run_and_exits_1(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() p, status := humustest.Start(t, runs(func(ctx context.Context) error { <-ctx.Done() return context.Cause(ctx) }), humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder()))) synctest.Wait() // the run is blocked on its context p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status require.Equal(t, humus.ExitFailure, st.Code()) require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), "serve: terminated signal received") spans := tel.Spans() require.Len(t, spans, 1) require.Equal(t, codes.Error, spans[0].Status().Code) require.Equal(t, "terminated signal received", spans[0].Status().Description) }) } The same test runs the end user’s own Init in place of runs, with the variables it reads set in humustest.WithEnv, such as EXPORT_BUCKET for the Init above.
Setting TRACEPARENT The run reads its trace context through the Process’s environment, so a test sets TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE with humustest.WithEnv, and reads the span’s trace ID and parent from the recorder:
_, status := humustest.Start(t, runs(func(ctx context.Context) error { schedule = baggage.FromContext(ctx).Member("schedule").Value() return nil }), humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), humustest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "TRACEPARENT": traceparent, "BAGGAGE": "schedule=nightly", }), ) require.Zero(t, (<-status).Code()) spans := tel.Spans() require.Len(t, spans, 1) span := spans[0] require.Equal(t, "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736", span.SpanContext().TraceID().String()) require.Equal(t, "00f067aa0ba902b7", span.Parent().SpanID().String()) require.True(t, span.Parent().IsRemote()) require.Equal(t, trace.SpanKindInternal, span.SpanKind()) require.Equal(t, "nightly", schedule) The Service contract job’s own tests hold job.Service to the Service contract with humustest.TestService, and a Service of your own that wraps a job is checked the same way. TestService needs a Service that runs until it is stopped, so the run blocks on its context:
func TestService_meets_the_Service_contract(t *testing.T) { humustest.TestService(t, func(t *testing.T, s *humus.Setup) humus.Service { return job.NewService(s, func(ctx context.Context) error { <-ctx.Done() return ctx.Err() }) }) } That exercises both stop paths: TestService’s rule that Serve returns nil after Shutdown relies on a bare Shutdown being reported as nil, and its rule for Shutdown after Serve has returned on its own cancels Serve’s context first.

humus packages are configured with plain Go values. They read no environment variables for their settings, define no variable names and read no files on your behalf; the few variables humus does read are listed below. Every value is sourced in your own Init, with whatever names and formats your service already uses: an environment variable called READ_TIMEOUT or MYSVC_HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT, a duration written 5s, a file of PEM, a flag. The usual tool is bedrock’s config package, and this page uses it throughout.
A framework that defined variable names would have to teach them, keep them consistent and document them twice. With Go values, godoc is the only documentation of a package’s settings, and a service’s variables are whatever its team chooses.
The design behind everything on this page is in the configuration revision of Proposal: configuration for humus apps.
What a package with settings exports Every humus package with settings exports the same three things:
a Settings struct, whose fields are plain values; DefaultSettings(), which returns the package’s defaults; a check function, Check<Field>, for each field that has a valid range. A zero field means zero, never “use the default”. A package’s defaults are the values DefaultSettings returns, and nothing else: a field left at zero is checked, and used, as zero. This keeps zero meaningful, as it is for net/http’s timeouts, where a zero ReadTimeout means no timeout.
The godoc of each field gives its default, its valid range and its meaning, and names its check. A check is a func(T) error. Its error says what is wrong, such as must not be negative, and does not name the field: whatever reads the value adds the name.
The samples on this page use a stand-in, declared in the root package’s tests in the shape every package gives it. The telemetry package’s Settings has the same shape, and Telemetry sources it with the same pattern, in the App’s telemetry Builder rather than in Init:
// Settings configures a Greeter. Every field is a plain value, and a field's // zero value means zero, never "use the default". type Settings struct { // Greeting is what the Greeter says. Default "hello". Greeting string // ReadTimeout bounds reading a whole request. Default 5s. Zero means // no timeout. Must not be negative; checked by CheckReadTimeout. ReadTimeout time.Duration // MaxConns is how many connections the Greeter serves at once. // Default 100. Must be positive; checked by CheckMaxConns. MaxConns int } // DefaultSettings returns the defaults of a Greeter. func DefaultSettings() Settings { return Settings{ Greeting: "hello", ReadTimeout: 5 * time.Second, MaxConns: 100, } } // CheckReadTimeout reports why d is not a valid ReadTimeout, or nil if it // is. func CheckReadTimeout(d time.Duration) error { if d < 0 { return errors.New("must not be negative") } return nil } // CheckMaxConns reports why n is not a valid MaxConns, or nil if it is. func CheckMaxConns(n int) error { if n <= 0 { return errors.New("must be positive") } return nil } In a real service these come from the package, as httpserver.Settings, httpserver.DefaultSettings() and httpserver.CheckReadTimeout, and you never copy a range out of godoc.
Sourcing Settings in Init Init reads the package’s Settings with config.Struct. Each field is one config.Value chain: where the value comes from, how it is parsed, .Default with the field of DefaultSettings(), and then the package’s check, chained with .Validate:
func GreeterInit(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) Settings { return Settings{ // The file is read as part of the setting, so a missing file // is a config error named after the variable. Greeting: r.Get(env("GREETING_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Default(d.Greeting)), ReadTimeout: r.Get(env("READ_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.ReadTimeout).Validate(CheckReadTimeout)), MaxConns: r.Get(env("MAX_CONNS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(d.MaxConns).Validate(CheckMaxConns)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78: every bad variable, one line each } g, err := NewGreeter(settings, s.Process.Stdout) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{g}, nil } The check goes after .Default, and the order matters for two reasons:
The default is checked too. A value that is not set is never checked, so a check chained before .Default would let a bad default through. Chained after it, a bad default fails exactly as a bad variable does. The error names the variable. A check in a field’s chain fails under that value’s name, so the error says READ_TIMEOUT, which is what an operator sets. A check on the whole struct could only name the field, ReadTimeout, which no operator sets. config.Struct attempts every Get, even after one has failed, so a misconfigured service reports all of its problems in one error rather than one per restart. Read every value through the Process and the Host in Setup, never through package os, so that the whole App runs in a test.
Reading a file A setting that names a file reads the file inside the field’s chain. Here GREETING_FILE is parsed by readFile, which opens the file through s.Host.FS:
// readFile returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that reads the whole // file a variable names, through fsys. func readFile(fsys humus.FS) func(name string) (string, error) { return func(name string) (string, error) { f, err := fsys.Open(name) if err != nil { return "", err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(f) return string(b), err } } Because the file is read as part of the setting, a missing or unreadable file is a config error named after its variable, and it exits 78 with the rest. humus.FS has no ReadFile: a helper this small is your code, not humus’s API, and it stays unexported. The same goes for decoding: a package takes a decoded value, such as a *tls.Config, never a path or a file’s contents, so how a certificate is stored and encoded is yours to decide. A further .Parse in the chain does the decoding.
How a bad value fails A bad value renders as config <variable>: <cause>. With READ_TIMEOUT=-5s and MAX_CONNS=lots, the App above logs both at ERROR through its telemetry, in one record of two lines, and exits 78:
init: config READ_TIMEOUT: must not be negative config MAX_CONNS: strconv.Atoi: parsing "lots": invalid syntax The lifecycle wraps the error Init returns once, as init: <error>, and logs it as it renders. config.Struct joins its failures with errors.Join, which renders one line per failure, so only the first line carries the init: prefix. Every line that names a bad variable starts config , prefix or not, and that is the word to search for.
And with GREETING_FILE naming a file that does not exist:
init: config GREETING_FILE: openat etc/greeter/greeting.txt: no such file or directory The cause is whatever the Host’s FS returned. This output is from the example, on a humustest Host, whose FS opens files through an os.Root, hence openat. On humus.OSHost() the same file fails with open <path>: no such file or directory.
Every error a config.Value returns is a *config.Error. When one is in the chain of the error Init returns, the App exits 78 (humus.ExitConfig, EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h), which tells an operator “fix the configuration” apart from “the service failed”. errors.AsType[*config.Error] finds the first bad variable in the chain, which is READ_TIMEOUT in the run above. A test that checks every bad variable walks the joined error, whose Unwrap() []error returns one *config.Error per variable, or compares the whole of the record the App logged. The lifecycle’s exit codes list the rest.
Building Settings in code config is a convenience, not a requirement. Settings can come from flags, a YAML file, or plain code:
settings := DefaultSettings() settings.ReadTimeout = -time.Second settings.MaxConns = 0 _, err := NewGreeter(settings, io.Discard) fmt.Println(err) A Settings built this way never passes through a check in a config chain, so the package’s constructor runs every check itself. It reports every bad field in one error, naming each field rather than a variable:
ReadTimeout: must not be negative MaxConns: must be positive The constructor of the stand-in shows the shape:
func NewGreeter(s Settings, out io.Writer) (*Greeter, error) { var errs []error if err := CheckReadTimeout(s.ReadTimeout); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("ReadTimeout: %w", err)) } if err := CheckMaxConns(s.MaxConns); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("MaxConns: %w", err)) } if err := errors.Join(errs...); err != nil { return nil, err } return &Greeter{settings: s, out: out}, nil } Its error is not a *config.Error, so an Init that returns it exits 1. A service that sources its settings with config and chains each check never reaches it: the bad value has already exited 78, named after its variable.
The variables humus reads humus reads the environment in two places, and neither is a setting of a package:
The lifecycle reads its two variables, HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY. humus.App.Run reads them before it calls Init, with defaults from App’s own fields, and checks each after its default, as on this page:
HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD defaults to the App’s ShutdownGracePeriod field: humus.Main’s 20s, or whatever an option, such as a runtime package’s defaults or humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod, or an App literal set it to. HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY, when it is set, replaces the App’s Drain, whatever that is, with humus.DrainDelay of its value, and adds a drain to an App that has none. When it is not set, the App’s Drain is the drain. The lifecycle’s settings describes them.
job reads the variables its propagator’s keys name. A job’s run joins the trace of the process that started it: job.Service extracts a trace context from the Process’s environment with the telemetry’s propagator, reading each of the propagator’s keys under the name OpenTelemetry’s environment-variable carriers give it. With telemetry.New’s propagator, those are TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE; a Builder with a propagator of another kind, such as B3, changes them. When none is set, or the value is malformed, the run starts a new trace and nothing fails. Jobs describes them.
Apart from the lifecycle’s two, humus still defines no variable names. The names job reads are OpenTelemetry’s: its specification names them, from the propagator’s keys, so a process that starts a job sets the same variables whatever language the job is written in. The telemetry package reads no OTEL_* variable either: a Builder that wants them maps them onto telemetry.Settings itself, as Telemetry shows.
Logging and secrets humus logs no settings, and it does not redact any. Whether to log the values a service started with, which ones, and how to hide a secret among them are your decisions. Init is given the same Process and Host that humus has, so it can log anything it wants, environment variables included, to s.Process.Stderr or to a logger of its own.
What humus does log is the error Init returns, through the App’s telemetry, and a parse error often quotes the value it could not parse: parsing "lots" above. A malformed secret, such as a token in the wrong format or a key that does not decode, would be logged the same way. Keeping a secret out of that error is part of the same choice: give the secret’s chain a parser of your own whose error says what is wrong without quoting the input.
Testing it Settings are tested by running the whole App with humustest.Start: humustest.WithEnv sets the variables, and a humustest Host holds the files the settings name. One of the root package’s examples runs the App above this way:
h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(files)) tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() p, status := humustest.Start(t, GreeterInit, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), humustest.WithEnv(env), ) st := <-status humus.WithHost replaces the Host Start builds with one the example made with its files, and humus.WithTelemetry passes humustest.Telemetry’s Builder, so the example prints the errors the App logged from the recorder’s Logs(). Both are humus’s own options, passed with humustest.WithApp as main passes them to humus.Main.
The App runs with Main’s defaults, so its grace period is Main’s 20s, as in production, and a HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD or HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY the test passes in WithEnv overrides it, as an operator’s would. WithEnv given twice keeps only the last map, so a test that adds to a base environment merges the maps itself, as Testing a humus App shows.
A relative name given to the humustest Host’s FS is relative to the test’s temp directory, and an absolute one, from h.Path, must be inside it, so a setting naming a file never reaches the real disk. Testing a humus App covers the Host in full.
